articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent millions on studies and consultants while drainage projects sit on a waitlist that grows longer each hurricane season.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.3 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but completed only 12 of 187 identified drainage projects
Engineering consultants have received $8.2 million while the county's own stormwater department remains understaffed by 40%
The project waitlist has grown from 142 sites in 2023 to 187 today, with some neighborhoods waiting since Hurricane Sally in 2020
articles.body:
The water pools in Marjorie Benton's front yard every time it rains more than half an inch. She has photographs going back to September 2020, when Hurricane Sally dropped two feet of water inside her Brent Lane home. Six years of documentation. Three different county commissioners. One stormwater fee she voted for and has paid every month since.

Her drainage ditch remains clogged. Her name sits at number 94 on a waitlist she didn't know existed until last month.

"They told me they'd get to it," Benton said. "That was 2021."

The Money Trail

Escambia County voters approved the stormwater utility fee in November 2022 by a margin of 58% to 42%. The pitch was straightforward: a dedicated funding stream for drainage infrastructure, separate from the general fund, immune to the budget battles that had starved maintenance for decades.

The fee took effect in January 2023. Residential property owners now pay $7.50 per month. Commercial rates vary by impervious surface area. The county projected $15 million annually.

It has delivered. Through March 2026, the stormwater utility has collected $47.3 million.

Where that money has gone is harder to track.

County budget documents obtained by The Flightline show $8.2 million paid to engineering consultants for master planning, watershed modeling, and project design. Another $4.1 million went to administrative costs—staff salaries, vehicles, software systems. Capital projects account for $11.7 million, though that figure includes land acquisition and equipment purchases alongside actual construction.

The remaining $23.3 million sits in reserve, designated for future projects that have not yet reached the construction phase.

"We're building capacity," said Marcus Webb, director of the county's stormwater management department, in an interview last week. "You can't just throw money at infrastructure. You need plans. You need engineering. You need to do this right."

Twelve Projects. One Hundred Eighty-Seven Waiting.

The county's 2023 stormwater master plan identified 142 drainage improvement sites across unincorporated Escambia County. Three years later, that list has grown to 187. Twelve projects have reached completion.

The math is not encouraging.

At the current pace, clearing the existing backlog would take 46 years. That assumes no new problems emerge—an assumption that Hurricane Helene, Hurricane Milton, and three unnamed tropical systems have already disproven.

The completed projects cluster in two areas: the Ferry Pass corridor along Mobile Highway and a section of Cantonment near Highway 29. Both areas had shovel-ready designs inherited from previous planning efforts. Both had vocal community advocates who showed up at commission meetings.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose District 1 includes several flooded neighborhoods in Perdido, has pressed for faster action. At an April 17 commission meeting, he asked Webb why communities impacted by Sally still await relief.

"I understand process," Bergosh said, according to meeting minutes. "I don't understand why process takes longer than the problem has existed."

Webb's response pointed to complexity. Watershed systems don't respect property lines. Fixing one drainage point can shift problems downstream. The master plan exists precisely to avoid that outcome.

Commissioner Steven Barry, whose District 5 contains some of the county's worst flooding, offered a different perspective.

"My constituents don't care about watershed modeling," Barry said. "They care about whether their kids can get to the school bus when it rains."

The Consultant Question

Atkins North America, a multinational engineering firm, holds the county's primary stormwater consulting contract. Since 2023, the company has received $5.4 million for master planning, design services, and project management.

A second firm, Baskerville-Donovan, has received $1.9 million for individual project designs. Three smaller firms split the remaining $900,000 in consulting fees.

These expenditures are not unusual. Counties across Florida rely heavily on outside engineering expertise for infrastructure work. What raises questions is the ratio.

For every dollar spent on consultants, the county has spent $1.43 on actual construction. Industry benchmarks typically show ratios closer to 1:4 or 1:5 for mature stormwater programs.

"We're front-loading the planning," Webb said. "Once we have designs in place, construction spending will accelerate."

The county's own stormwater department tells a different story. Of 15 budgeted engineering positions, nine are filled. The department has struggled to compete with private-sector salaries that often exceed county pay grades by 30% or more.

Webb acknowledged the staffing gap but said it makes outside consultants more necessary, not less.

What Voters Were Promised

Campaign materials from the 2022 stormwater fee referendum, archived by the Escambia County Supervisor of Elections, made specific commitments.

"Your fee dollars will go directly to drainage improvements in your community," one mailer read. "No more waiting. No more excuses."

A television advertisement featured footage of flooded streets and a voiceover promising "real solutions, not more studies."

Three years later, studies represent 17% of total expenditures. Construction represents 25%. Reserves represent 49%.

County Administrator Wes Moreno defended the spending pattern at a budget workshop in March.

"Reserves are not waste," Moreno said. "They're projects waiting to happen. We're being fiscally responsible."

Fiscal responsibility is not the complaint from Brent Lane, Perdido Key, or Cantonment. Speed is.

The Growing List

New problem sites continue to emerge faster than old ones get fixed.

Hurricane Helene in September 2024 added 22 locations to the drainage complaint database. Tropical Storm unnamed systems in 2025 added 14 more. Development activity in the northern part of the county has created runoff issues in areas that previously drained adequately.

The master plan contemplates a 20-year buildout. At current collection rates and spending patterns, the county would amass roughly $300 million in stormwater fees over that period. The estimated cost to address all identified drainage deficiencies: $412 million, according to the 2023 plan.

That gap assumes no inflation, no new problems, and no major storms. Assumptions that Florida weather does not support.

"The fee was never going to fix everything," said Doug Underhill, a former county commissioner who supported the referendum. "But it was supposed to fix something. People are right to ask what they're getting."

What Happens Next

The commission's next budget workshop is scheduled for June 12. Stormwater spending is on the agenda.

Commissioner Barry has proposed shifting $10 million from reserves into immediate construction contracts, targeting the 20 oldest items on the project waitlist. The proposal has not yet received a second.

Commissioner Bergosh has suggested hiring a third-party auditor to review consultant expenditures and staffing efficiency. That proposal also awaits support.

Webb's department plans to release an updated project timeline in July. The document will show which neighborhoods can expect construction in 2027, 2028, and beyond.

Marjorie Benton will look for her address on that list. She has been looking for three years.

"I did what they asked," she said. "I voted for the fee. I pay the fee. I call the office. I show up at meetings. What else am I supposed to do?"

She gestured at her front yard, still muddy from last week's thunderstorms.

"Wait, I guess. That's what they keep telling me. Wait."

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: The Last Fish House on Joe Patti's Block
articles.dek: As waterfront land values soar and developers circle, one family operation holds out on the working waterfront that made Pensacola's seafood reputation.
brief: The Ramos family fish house is the last independent seafood operation on the block where Joe Patti's built Pensacola's commercial fishing reputation
Waterfront property values along the A Street corridor have tripled since 2019, with developers proposing condos and mixed-use projects on former fish house lots
The family has rejected multiple seven-figure offers but faces mounting pressure from rising insurance costs and shrinking access to commercial dock space
articles.body:
At 4:47 a.m. on a Tuesday in late April, Carmen Ramos stands in rubber boots on a concrete floor slick with ice melt and fish blood. Behind her, a chest freezer hums. In front of her, through a roll-up door facing Pensacola Bay, the sky is still black. A shrimp boat is coming in.

"You can smell them before you see them," she says. "That's how you know they had a good trip."

The Ramos Fish Company has occupied this cinder block building at 620 South A Street for 31 years. Carmen's father, Luis Ramos, bought it in 1995 from an oysterman who'd gone broke. Back then, this stretch of waterfront between Main Street and Joe Patti's Seafood held eight independent fish houses. Boats unloaded at dawn. Trucks pulled out by noon carrying mullet for Mississippi smokeries, red snapper for Atlanta restaurants, grouper for the frozen food aisle at Winn-Dixie.

Now the Ramos operation is alone.

The Block That Built a Reputation

The working waterfront along South A Street shaped Pensacola's identity as a commercial fishing port for the better part of a century. The Patti family opened their retail market in 1931. Smaller operations clustered nearby, buying catch from boats too small to deal with large distributors, processing fish for local restaurants and grocery stores, keeping ice houses running and nets mended.

By the early 2000s, the math started turning against them.

"Insurance went up. Property taxes went up. The boats started going to Bayou La Batre instead because the fuel was cheaper," says Mike Murdock, a former deckhand who worked the docks here through the 1990s. "And then people figured out you could see the water from these lots."

The Escambia County Property Appraiser's office shows the pattern clearly. In 2019, the assessed value of waterfront commercial property along the A Street corridor averaged $38 per square foot. By 2025, that figure had climbed to $127 per square foot. The lot directly north of Ramos Fish Company—formerly Tidewater Seafood, which closed in 2021—sold last year for $2.1 million. The buyer was a Destin-based development group.

Planning documents filed with the City of Pensacola show a proposed 48-unit condominium project for the site. Groundbreaking is scheduled for fall 2026.

Seven Figures, Seven Times

Carmen Ramos, 44, took over daily operations from her father three years ago. Luis, now 71, still comes in most mornings to check the books and drink coffee from a styrofoam cup. His hands shake slightly when he holds it.

The family has received seven written offers to purchase the property since 2022. Carmen keeps them in a manila folder in her office, a plywood-walled room roughly the size of a walk-in closet. The highest offer, dated January 2026, came from a Tampa investment group: $3.4 million for the lot and building, with a 60-day close.

"They wanted an answer in two weeks," Carmen says. "I told them we've been here 31 years. Two weeks isn't how we make decisions."

She declined that offer, as she had the six before it.

The calculus is not purely sentimental. The Ramos operation clears between $180,000 and $240,000 annually, according to financial disclosures the family provided for this article. Carmen draws a salary of $52,000. Her father takes $30,000. Three full-time employees split the rest. The building is paid off. The business has no debt.

"We're not getting rich," Carmen says. "But we're not drowning either. Not yet."

The Pressure Points

What threatens the operation now is not any single crisis but an accumulation of smaller ones.

Commercial insurance for the property has increased 67% since 2022, from $28,000 annually to $46,800 in 2026. The building sits in a FEMA-designated flood zone, which limits refinancing options and requires separate flood coverage.

Access to commercial dock space has also tightened. The Ramos fish house shares a pier with two other properties. One of those properties sold last year. The new owner, a Pensacola architect, has filed preliminary plans for a private residence with a recreational boat slip. If that project moves forward, the shared commercial dock agreement—signed in 1987—faces legal challenge.

"The lawyer says we have rights," Carmen says. "But hiring a lawyer costs money. Going to court costs money. And the whole time, you're not focused on the business."

Then there are the boats themselves. The Ramos operation buys from a rotating group of roughly 15 commercial fishing vessels, most of them owner-operated boats under 40 feet. That fleet is aging and shrinking. Two captains retired last year. One moved his operation to Panama City. No new boats have joined the rotation since 2023.

What Remains

On a busy morning, the Ramos fish house moves between 800 and 1,200 pounds of seafood. Mullet goes to a smokery in Biloxi. Grouper and snapper sell to five Pensacola restaurants, including a long-standing account with Jackson's Steakhouse. Shrimp, when available, goes to a small network of retail customers who show up at the loading dock with coolers.

The retail sales happen without signage, advertising, or any online presence. Word of mouth only.

"Joe Patti's has the tourists," Carmen says. "We have the people who've been coming here since before the tourists knew where Pensacola was."

One of those customers is Delores Washington, 68, who arrives at 7 a.m. most Saturdays in a maroon Buick. She has been buying mullet from the Ramos family since 1999.

"My husband used to fish with Luis," Washington says, standing at the loading dock with a blue cooler at her feet. "Now my husband's gone and Luis is almost gone and this place is almost gone. Everything's almost gone."

She pauses. "But it's not gone yet."

The View From the Water

At 6:15 a.m., the shrimp boat ties up at the shared dock. Captain Ray Dominguez has been running this route for 22 years. His boat, the Santa Maria II, is a 38-foot wooden trawler built in 1986. The hull needs work. The outriggers creak.

"I could sell to the processors in Bayou La Batre," Dominguez says, standing on the dock while his deckhand shovels ice into plastic totes. "But then I'm just a number. Here, I'm Ray. My fish are my fish."

He hauls 340 pounds of brown shrimp this morning, plus 80 pounds of bycatch—mostly croaker and spot. Carmen inspects the catch, makes notes on a clipboard, and hands Dominguez a check written from a pad she keeps in her back pocket. No electronic payment. No app. No invoice emailed later.

"This is how it worked in 1995," she says. "This is how it works now."

Whether it works in 2030 is another question.

No Exit Strategy

Luis Ramos does not speak to reporters often. He agreed to a brief conversation for this article, conducted in his daughter's office while she processed the morning's catch.

Asked why he doesn't sell, he takes a long time to answer.

"Sell to who?" he finally says. "To someone who tears it down? Then what? Another condo nobody lives in? Another restaurant that closes in two years?"

He gestures toward the water, visible through the open roll-up door.

"This is a working waterfront. That's what it is. That's what it's supposed to be. The boats come in. The fish go out. That's the deal. That's always been the deal."

He shakes his head. "You don't sell the deal."

Carmen, for her part, has no succession plan. She has no children. Her brother lives in Houston and has no interest in the business. The question of what happens after her is one she declines to answer directly.

"I think about it," she says. "I don't have an answer. But I'm not going to make a decision based on not having an answer. That's not how we do things."

Outside, the sun is finally up. The shrimp boat pulls away from the dock, heading back toward the pass. A pelican lands on a piling and watches the fish house with what looks like professional interest.

Carmen Ramos goes back to work.

articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 200,000 Visitors and a Familiar Debate
articles.dek: Hotel taxes will spike, traffic will gridlock, and city officials will once again sidestep questions about whether Pensacola sees a dime of the economic impact it advertises.
brief: The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show returns to NAS Pensacola this weekend, with Visit Pensacola projecting 200,000 attendees and $50 million in economic impact
Despite the tourism windfall, the City of Pensacola receives no direct revenue from the event—all tourist development taxes flow to Escambia County
City officials have declined to answer repeated questions about cost-sharing arrangements for public safety and infrastructure strain during the three-day event
articles.body:
The jets will scream over Bayou Grande starting Thursday morning. Practice runs, then the real thing. By Saturday afternoon, an estimated 200,000 people will pack the flight line at Naval Air Station Pensacola, necks craned, phones raised, watching six F/A-18 Super Hornets trace impossible geometries against the Gulf Coast sky.

This is Homecoming Week. The crown jewel of Pensacola's tourism calendar. The weekend that fills every hotel room from Perdido Key to Tiger Point and turns Palafox Street into a sea of navy blue t-shirts.

It is also, depending on who you ask, either the best economic engine the region has or a three-day exercise in municipal cost-shifting that Pensacola taxpayers subsidize without seeing a direct return.

The $50 Million Question

Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing arm, released its annual projections last week. The numbers are familiar: 200,000 total visitors, $50 million in direct economic impact, hotel occupancy rates approaching 98 percent across the county.

"Blue Angels Homecoming is the single largest tourism event in Northwest Florida," said Dana Young, Visit Pensacola's president and CEO. "The economic ripple effects touch virtually every sector of our hospitality industry."

Those ripple effects generate tourist development tax revenue. Escambia County collects a 5 percent levy on short-term rentals—hotel rooms, vacation homes, Airbnbs. During a typical Homecoming weekend, that translates to roughly $400,000 in additional TDT collections, according to county budget documents.

That money flows to Escambia County. Not to the City of Pensacola.

This is how Florida law works. Tourist development taxes are county-level instruments. Municipalities don't get a cut unless the county chooses to share. Escambia County has not chosen to share.

Who Pays for the Party

The City of Pensacola, meanwhile, bears measurable costs.

Pensacola Police Department deploys additional officers for traffic control along the downtown corridors that serve as primary arteries to NAS Pensacola's back gate. The department has not released specific overtime figures for Homecoming Week, but PPD spokesperson Mike Wood confirmed that "significant additional resources" are allocated.

The city's public works department handles increased sanitation demands downtown. Parks and recreation staff manage overflow parking at city facilities. Code enforcement responds to complaints about unpermitted vacation rentals that proliferate during peak tourism weekends.

Asked whether the city tracks aggregate costs associated with Blue Angels Homecoming, Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves' office did not respond to three separate inquiries over two weeks.

City Council President Allison Scott referred questions to the mayor's office. Council member Jennifer Brahier said she was "not aware of any formal cost analysis" but would "welcome that conversation."

Council member Casey Jones, whose District 6 includes much of the traffic-impacted West Side, was more direct.

"I've asked about this," Jones said. "I haven't gotten answers I find satisfying. The county advertises the economic impact. The city absorbs costs. Somewhere there should be a balance sheet."

The Familiar Deflection

This is not a new debate. It resurfaces every May, briefly, then subsides beneath the roar of jet engines and the genuine civic pride that accompanies watching the world's most famous flight demonstration team perform in its own backyard.

The Blue Angels have been based at NAS Pensacola since 1954. Homecoming—the team's final show of the season, performed at their home station—carries emotional weight that transcends municipal accounting.

"You can't put a dollar figure on what the Blue Angels mean to this community," said retired Navy Captain Tom Moreau, who flew with the team from 2008 to 2010 and now lives in East Hill. "The pride, the heritage, the connection to naval aviation history—that's Pensacola's identity."

This is true. It is also a reliable pivot when questions about money arise.

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes much of Pensacola proper, defended the current arrangement at a commission meeting last month.

"The economic impact benefits everyone," Bergosh said. "Pensacola businesses see increased revenue. Pensacola residents have jobs in the hospitality industry. The TDT dollars get reinvested in tourism promotion that keeps this cycle going."

He did not address whether county funds offset city costs. A follow-up request for comment was not returned.

Traffic, Parking, and the Annual Ritual

For residents of Warrington, Myrtle Grove, and the West Side neighborhoods nearest NAS Pensacola, Homecoming Week means something more immediate than economic impact studies.

It means gridlock.

Navy Boulevard becomes impassable for hours on Saturday afternoon. Blue Angel Parkway backs up past the Walmart. Side streets transform into de facto parking lots as visitors abandon their cars wherever space exists.

"Last year I couldn't get out of my own driveway for three hours," said Maria Santos, who has lived on Fairfield Drive for 22 years. "I'm not against the air show. But nobody asks us if we're okay with this."

NAS Pensacola public affairs officer Lieutenant Commander Bryce Alderson said the base coordinates with local law enforcement and encourages attendees to arrive early and carpool.

"We recognize the impact on surrounding communities," Alderson said. "We try to be good neighbors. But ultimately we have 200,000 people trying to access a single location in a compressed timeframe. There are limits to what traffic management can achieve."

The Number Nobody Mentions

There is another figure that rarely appears in the glossy economic impact reports.

The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show is a free event. NAS Pensacola charges no admission. The Navy covers operational costs. Visit Pensacola covers marketing.

The $50 million in economic impact is real money spent by real visitors at real businesses. But it is diffuse. It flows to hotels and restaurants and gas stations and souvenir shops across two counties. Much of it flows to national chains—Marriott, Hilton, Applebee's—whose profits leave the region entirely.

What stays? What accrues to local governments to offset the costs of hosting? How much of that $50 million translates to tax revenue that funds the public services strained by 200,000 additional people?

Visit Pensacola does not track this. Escambia County does not publish this. The City of Pensacola, apparently, does not calculate this.

"Economic impact" is not the same as "fiscal impact." The former is a marketing number. The latter is an accounting number. Pensacola advertises one and ignores the other.

Thursday Morning

The jets will take off around 11 a.m. for practice. They will arc over the bay, bank hard over the beach, pull vertical over downtown. The sound will rattle windows in East Hill and Scenic Heights and all the way out to Cordova Park.

People will stop what they're doing and look up. They always do.

For those few seconds, the accounting questions won't matter. The jurisdictional squabbles will fade. There will just be six blue-and-gold jets against a cloudless sky, doing impossible things, representing something that transcends line items and tax distributions.

Then the sound will fade. Traffic will build. The hotels will fill. The money will flow in directions that nobody in city government seems willing to trace.

And next May, we'll have this conversation again.
